title: A target isn't set up to be missed
hookLine: evil isn't built into nature, any more than a target is set up to be missed (Enchiridion 27)

lines: NOBODY HANGS A TARGET TO BE MISSED.
cards: At an archery range, the targets stand in a row: straw bales, painted rings, a gold circle in the middle. Some arrows land in the gold. Many land in the outer rings, the grass, the fence behind.
But nobody hangs a target hoping it will be missed. It exists to be hit. The misses are real, sometimes lots of them, but they aren't what the target is for.
Section twenty-seven of the handbook is one puzzling sentence built on that picture.

teach.h: NOT SET UP TO BE MISSED.
teach.b: Here's the sentence. Just as a target isn't set up in order to be missed, Epictetus says, so the nature of evil doesn't arise in the world. That's all.
No example, no explanation. Now the honest part: readers still argue about this line, and nobody can be sure exactly what he meant.
Two readings have lasted. One, from the ancient commentator Simplicius and others: the world is ordered toward the good, the way a target is set up to be hit. Evil isn't one of its built-in parts.

It's a missing, a falling short, real but not the point. Two, a more practical reading: in the world outside us, nothing is truly evil, because for a Stoic the only real evil is a bad choice in a person's own will.
Either way, the mark is there to be aimed at.
The Greek for target is skopos, the mark an archer fixes the eye on. The picture doesn't deny the misses; the grass behind a range is full of arrows. It says they aren't why the target is there.
A miss only counts as a miss because there's a mark to measure it by. Whatever the metaphysics, the practice is simple. A miss doesn't mean the target was a lie.
Yesterday's sharp word, last week's broken promise: arrows in the grass. The gold is still there.

how: Some Stoic practitioners treat mistakes as misses rather than proof that the good is out of reach, and choose a specific good to aim at each day.

games.q: you've missed the mark badly this week. on the target picture, what follows?
o: the target is still there; pick up another arrow.
games.why: a target isn't set up to be missed. the misses are real, but the gold is still there to aim at.

practice: Picture a target, the gold circle clear in the middle, and put one small, specific good in it: a patient answer, a finished task, a kind word to someone who's hard to like.
Let one recent miss lie in the grass without picking it up to examine it. Then breathe in, and draw back an imaginary bow toward the gold.
